title: Graded Degradation: Sales & CS Cheatsheet
content:
Purpose
This is a compact, pragmatic cheatsheet for Sales, Customer Success, and Solutions Engineers to explain Redwood’s graded-degradation approach to reliability. Goal: give short, consistent narratives and scripts you can use in discovery calls, renewal conversations, security reviews, and post-incident outreach.

Context / quick thesis
- Customers care more about predictable outcomes than perfect uptime; they want to know what will happen and how we’ll make it safe.
- ‘Graded degradation’ is the controlled set of behaviors Redwood will perform when a resource, model, or region is constrained. It minimizes customer impact while preserving core functionality and transparency.
- This is not reactive marketing — it’s a set of prescriptive, verifiable behaviors we can point to in contracts, runbooks, and dashboards.

Top-level one-liner for sales pitches
- "If capacity, models, or regions are constrained, Redwood will silently route to the next best compatible option or fall back into a safe, reduced-quality mode with clear indicators so your application stays online and auditable."

Key benefits to emphasize (short bullets for customers)
- Continuity: Customers stay online (reduced features preferred to complete outage).
- Predictability: Pre-defined policies determine fallback behavior — not ad-hoc engineering choices during incidents.
- Observability: Token-level cost/latency attribution, incident timelines, and automated post-incident summaries.
- Compliance-friendly: VPC/private deployment fallbacks, encrypted KMS keys retained; we can prove data residency/segregation during rollbacks.

Fallback patterns (explain simply)
- Model variant fallback: If your pinned Llama3-34B-quant can’t be scheduled, we attempt a smaller verified variant (Llama3-13B-quant) with degradation guidance (e.g., lower context fidelity).
- Multi-region reroute: If eu-west region is degraded, requests are routed to eu-central then us-west based on policy (latency threshold + data residency constraints).
- Feature gating (degraded UX): For chat apps, preserve core delivery (answers) but disable heavy analysis features (summarization, long-context retrieval) until capacity recovers.
- Queue & backpressure: For burst overloads, short queuing with user-visible ETA and progressive responses rather than dropping requests.

Short incident narratives (templates you can read aloud or paste into email)
- Initial alert (to customer): "We detected elevated latency in eu-west affecting throughput for model X. Our control plane activated fallback policy A: traffic routed to eu-central and a verified smaller model. You may see slightly shorter/concise responses for ~22 minutes while capacity scales. No data was redirected outside approved regions."
- If persistent (follow-up): "After 2 hours we observed continued pressure; we escalated to Dedicated burst and initiated model reshuffle. We will provide a 1-hour postmortem and a compensation estimate if SLA targets were missed."
- In tightly regulated contexts: "We did not route traffic outside the approved VPC. The degradation was handled within your Dedicated pool using reduced batching to satisfy latency SLOs. Detailed audit logs are attached."

Trust language — what to avoid and preferred phrasing
- Avoid vague absolutes: Don’t say "never" or "guarantee" outside of contractual SLA lanes.
- Prefer concrete, verifiable statements: "We will route to the next approved region/model according to your routing policy and log all decisions."
- Use measurable attributes: latency windows, expected quality delta (e.g., "~10-20% shorter summaries"), expected duration range, and follow-up deliverables (postmortem, mitigation plan).

Customer-facing scripts for common scenarios
- Discovery call (customer asks about outages): "We handle incidents with a graded plan: failover, model fallback, and a degraded feature mode, prioritized by your business-critical routes. Most customers prefer graceful degradation over sudden outages because it keeps the product usable while preserving user trust."
- Renewal / trust reinforcement: "During the last quarter we had 1 incident affecting <0.1% requests; our automated fallbacks kept customer traffic alive and our post-incident review delivered a targeted fix to eliminate the root cause. We include the incident summary in the renewal pack."
- Security/compliance review: "We maintain an auditable trail for every fallback decision. For Private/Dedicated customers, fallbacks operate inside your boundaries; we provide the audit logs and signed attestations as required."

Objection handling quick-notes
- "But routing across regions can break compliance" → "We will not route outside allowed regions for customers that require residency — fallback will use local Dedicated capacity or a reduced feature mode inside the same region."
- "Fallbacks hurt quality" → "We provide verified downgrade profiles showing expected output delta and an option to pin model versions or decline certain fallback types."
- "Will fallbacks increase cost?" → "There are configurable policies: cost-first, latency-first, and strict-isolation. You choose tradeoffs via Console and we can show projected unit economics for each policy."

Operational artifacts to reference (internal shorthand)
- Runbook: INF-2891 (model-fallback-runbook)
- Policy editor demo: Console > Deployments > Routing Policies (use demo tenant GTM-DEMO-004)
- Monitoring dashboards: Console -> Observability -> Fallbacks by Route (token-level)

Metrics to share with customers (what they care about)
- % requests routed to fallback in last 30 days (goal: <0.5% for Hosted customers)
- Mean additional latency introduced by reroute (ms)
- % of incidents that resulted in degraded-mode vs full outage
- Time to automatic recovery and time to human mitigation

Examples / quick evidence for technical buyers
- Post-incident timeline snippet: "2025-07-03 14:12 UTC — traffic spike; 14:14 — automated cascade: model fallback to M-13B-quant; 14:25 — multi-region routing to eu-central; 14:40 — autoscale added Dedicated burst; 14:55 — traffic returned to baseline."
- Short QA result: "We run synthetic queries to validate fallbacks during weekday maintenance windows; expected semantic similarity vs primary model measured at 0.82 average — documented in CONFLUENCE: GTM/Degradation-Model-Benchmarks."

Open questions / decisions to make (internal)
- Default upgrade for sales demos: enable multi-region fallback by default? (PRO: demo resilience; CON: may obscure residency constraints)
- Should we publish short public-facing matrix that maps fallback mode → expected quality delta for top-selling models?
- Standard compensation thresholds for Hosted (when fallback exceeds X% of requests in billing period).

Immediate next steps (owner list)
- Priya: finalize this cheatsheet and push to Sales playbook (GTM-4123).
- Connor: add two call-ready slides (fallback flow diagram + one-line metrics) for AE enablement deck.
- Elena: add 3 canned incident emails to the CS templates repo.
- Samir: coordinate with Product to define default routing policy for demo tenants.

Notes to self (informal)
- Keep scripts short — customers want clarity.
- Add real examples from last quarter postmortems to the public-facing FAQ once legal signs off.
- Link to compensation policy and SLA text when referencing credits.

---
End of cheatsheet. Pasteable snippets are above for quick copy/paste into email or slack. Use the runbook IDs and dashboards cited when you need technical backup.
